choices: A low initial price to build a critical mass of customers
An incumbent keeping price below the monopoly level to prevent entry
A firm temporarily pricing below marginal cost to drive competitors out of the market
Charging different prices to different customers

stem: What is the usual legal test for the 'below cost' part of a predatory pricing case?
choices: Price below average total cost of the rival
explain: Slide p. 46: the usual legal test is below average variable cost.

stem: Under Brooke Group (1993), what must be shown besides pricing below cost?
choices: That the rival was more efficient
That prices were above the monopoly level
That the firm had a patent
explain: Below cost plus a dangerous probability of recouping the losses (slide p. 46).

stem: True or false: Predatory pricing means accepting losses now in the hope of recouping them with higher prices after the rival exits.
True or false: Predatory pricing targets potential entrants who have not yet entered.
explain: False. It targets a rival already in the market. Potential entrants are the target of limit pricing.

stem: Which law can predatory pricing violate?
choices: No law; it is always legal
explain: Slide p. 46: it can violate Sherman Act §2.

stem: Why is predatory pricing hard to prove?
choices: It only happens in regulated industries
Aggressive but legal competition also produces low prices
explain: Low prices are usually good for consumers, so courts need evidence of below-cost pricing and likely recoupment.

stem: According to the textbook, which situation makes predatory pricing most likely to pay off?
choices: A rival that can easily shut down and reopen
A market with very low entry barriers
A deep-pocketed firm against a cash-strapped rival, with little chance of re-entry
explain: The predator must outlast the prey and then keep others out long enough to recoup.

stem: After a predator drives out its rival, what can undermine the payoff?
choices: The rival re-enters, or someone buys its assets and comes back
explain: If entry returns once prices rise, the predator cannot recoup its losses.

stem: A taxi company sued Uber, claiming Uber priced rides below cost to drive taxis out of San Francisco (slides p. 44). What type of claim is this?
explain: The rivals (taxis) were already in the market, and the claim is below-cost pricing to drive them out.

stem: A national chain sells hammers at $6 next to a local store when the hammers cost the chain $9, planning to raise prices once the local store closes. Classify it.
explain: Below cost, aimed at an existing rival, with recoupment planned.

stem: A new food delivery app charges $0 delivery for its first year, below its cost, to get people to try it in a city where an established app dominates. Is this predatory pricing?
choices: Yes, because the incumbent is hurt
Probably not; it is penetration pricing aimed at building a customer base
Yes, any below-cost price is predatory
explain: A newcomer pricing low (even free) to win customers is penetration pricing. Predatory pricing is aimed at driving a rival out and recouping later.

stem: A firm cuts its price from $40 to $30. Its average variable cost is $25. An entrant has not yet come in. Is this predatory pricing?
choices: Yes: any price cut is predatory
No: price is above cost and the target is a potential entrant, so it is limit pricing
explain: Predatory pricing requires below-cost pricing aimed at an existing rival.

stem: In the textbook, Microsoft gave Internet Explorer away free and tied it to Windows to cut off Netscape. What was the outcome?
choices: Netscape was found guilty of predatory pricing
explain: Microsoft lost the suit, and the EU later ruled the tying illegal.
